name: Fisher's Principle
statement: Natural selection pushes the sex ratio toward an even split.
meaning: In most sexually reproducing species, selection drives the ratio of males to females toward one to one, because parents are favoured for investing equally in sons and daughters. Whichever sex is currently rarer offers better mating prospects, so producing more of it pays — until the advantage vanishes at balance.
mechanism: It works by negative frequency-dependent selection. Every offspring has exactly one mother and one father, so each sex contributes half the genes of the next generation. If one sex becomes scarce, each of its members has, on average, more mates, so parents with a heritable tendency to over-produce the rarer sex leave more grandchildren, and that tendency spreads. The advantage disappears precisely at one to one, making it the stable equilibrium. Strictly, selection equalises total parental expenditure on each sex; when a son and a daughter cost the same to raise, equal expenditure means equal numbers.

examples.text: Most outbred mammals and birds show sex ratios close to one to one — humans included, with a slight, well-documented male bias at birth of about 1.05, a near-Fisherian case.

Parasitoid wasps such as Nasonia produce strongly female-biased broods when offspring mate among themselves before dispersing — exactly where Fisher's assumption of population-wide random mating fails, so the model correctly predicts its own departures.
Where one sex is cheaper to produce, equal expenditure yields unequal numbers — the balance is struck in cost, and only reduces to a numerical even split when the two sexes cost the same.

variants.name: Local mate competition
variants.text: Hamilton's 1967 refinement: when relatives compete for mates in structured, inbred groups, adaptive female-biased ratios evolve, as in fig and parasitoid wasps.

variants.name: The Trivers-Willard hypothesis
variants.text: A conditional extension predicting that parents in good versus poor condition should bias offspring sex, distinct from Fisher's population-level equilibrium.

whyItMatters: It is a cornerstone of sex-allocation theory and, in A. W. F. Edwards's phrase, 'probably the most celebrated argument in evolutionary biology' — a rare case where a qualitative selection argument yields a sharp quantitative prediction, whose confirmed exceptions map its assumptions precisely.

working.text: in a large outbred population with equally costly sexes, predict a roughly even sex ratio as the evolutionary equilibrium.
when the sexes differ in cost, predict equal expenditure — which can mean unequal numbers.
where mating is local or inbred, expect female-biased ratios, as local mate competition predicts.

limits: It predicts equal investment, not always equal numbers, and holds under specific assumptions — random mating, an outbred population, and no differential sex costs. Biased ratios arise wherever those break: local mate competition in structured or inbred populations favours female bias; haplodiploidy lets mothers control offspring sex precisely, enabling extreme skews; selfish genetic elements and meiotic drive can distort ratios against the parental optimum; and environmental sex determination sets the ratio by ecology rather than allocation.
misreadings: It is not a claim that sex ratios are always exactly even — it predicts equal parental investment, which only equals equal numbers when the sexes cost the same, and it is routinely overridden where its assumptions fail. Nor is the even ratio for the good of the species: it emerges from selection on individual parents.
origin: Named for Ronald A. Fisher, who stated it in The Genetical Theory of Natural Selection (1930); Charles Darwin gave essentially the same reasoning in the first edition of The Descent of Man (1871) but removed it later, and Carl Dusing had formalised it mathematically in 1883-1884.

sources.text: Fisher's principle, Wikipedia. — the even-ratio argument, equal investment, local mate competition, and the Darwin/Dusing precedence.
Edwards, A. W. F. "Carl Dusing (1884) on the regulation of the sex-ratio," Theoretical Population Biology 58(3):255-257 (2000), PubMed. — the Dusing precedence and the argument's history.
